key_patterns.name: Temporal persistence (habit/inertia)
key_patterns.description: Agents who wore a mask on day t-1 are more likely to wear a mask on day t than those who did not (state dependence).
key_patterns.relevance: Supports inclusion of a persistence parameter or habit term in the adoption rule; improves short-term predictability.

key_patterns.name: Information-driven adoption
key_patterns.description: Exposure to pro-mask information on day t-1 increases the probability of adopting/wearing on day t, controlling for prior state.
key_patterns.relevance: Calibrates the effect size of exogenous information campaigns and helps disentangle peer vs. external influence.

key_patterns.name: Networked social influence
key_patterns.description: The fraction of neighbors wearing masks correlates with an agent’s likelihood to wear on the next day.
key_patterns.relevance: Justifies a threshold/contagion term using neighbor adoption signals; enables layer-specific influence weights.

key_patterns.name: Heterogeneity by risk_perception
key_patterns.description: Higher risk_perception associates with higher baseline adoption and/or lower required neighbor threshold to adopt.
key_patterns.relevance: Supports agent-level heterogeneity in thresholds or baseline propensities derived from risk_perception.

key_patterns.name: Demographic/context stratification
key_patterns.description: Adoption and responsiveness differ by age_group and occupation (e.g., students shaped by school layer, workers by workplace layer).
key_patterns.relevance: Motivates group-specific multipliers and layer weights; guides reporting and targeted interventions.

key_patterns.name: Multiplex structure and homophily
key_patterns.description: Family, work/school, and community layers have different degrees, clustering, and likely homophily by age_group and occupation.
key_patterns.relevance: Requires layer-specific contact frequencies and influence weights; homophily affects cascade thresholds and speed.

key_distributions.name: Risk perception distribution
key_distributions.description: Continuous values in [0,1]; often well-approximated by a Beta distribution.

key_distributions.name: Layer-specific degree distributions
key_distributions.description: Per-layer node degrees from social_network.json (family low/mid, work_school moderate, community skewed).
key_distributions.parameters: For each layer L in {family, work_school, community}: mean degree kbar_L, variance var_L, tail index or lognormal params

key_distributions.name: Initial mask prevalence
key_distributions.description: Day-0 wearing_mask prevalence overall and by subgroup (age_group, occupation).

key_distributions.name: Daily information exposure rate
key_distributions.description: Probability an agent receives pro-mask info per day; possibly time-varying and group-specific.

key_distributions.name: Adoption thresholds / susceptibility
key_distributions.description: Distribution of individual thresholds or susceptibilities to neighbor influence.
key_distributions.parameters: Threshold distribution parameters (e.g., Beta(a_thr, b_thr)) or susceptibility coefficients by layer

key_relationships.strength: To estimate via transition probabilities or logistic regression

key_relationships.relationship: Positive effect of information exposure on adoption the next day (and possibly same day).
key_relationships.strength: To estimate; check for immediate and lag-1 effects

key_relationships.relationship: Higher neighbor adoption increases own adoption likelihood (network externality).
key_relationships.strength: To estimate overall and by layer weights

key_relationships.relationship: Higher risk_perception linked to higher baseline wearing and/or lower thresholds.
key_relationships.strength: To estimate; include interaction with network exposure

key_relationships.relationship: Group differences in baseline, responsiveness to info, and peer effects.
key_relationships.strength: To estimate; use fixed effects or group-specific coefficients

time_step_days.notes: Use synchronous daily updates of agent states.

update_scheme.notes: Compute neighbor influence from t and update all agents to t+1.

layer_handling.notes: Maintain separate graphs per layer; allow overlaps.

edge_directionality.notes: Symmetrize adjacency; remove self-loops and deduplicate.

layer_contact_weights.notes: Weights w_family ≥ w_work_school ≥ w_community expected; calibrate to match stratified dynamics.

degree_statistics.notes: Use for contact sampling and sensitivity to network sparsity.

homophily_mixing_matrix.notes: Compute assortativity by age_group and occupation to inform diffusion heterogeneity.

risk_perception_prior.notes: Fit Beta via MLE or method of moments.

initial_mask_state.notes: If missing day 0, use earliest observed day as initialization.

baseline_propensity.notes: Estimate alpha0, alpha_r from panel data with no-neighbor/no-info subset or via regression.

habit_persistence.notes: Empirically estimate transition probabilities; map to persistence coefficient gamma.

info_effect.notes: Estimate immediate and lagged effects; allow decay if multi-day effects observed.

network_influence_strength.notes: Estimate via logistic model using neighbor_mask_fraction_t-1 overall and per layer.

layer_specific_weights.notes: Calibrate such that combined exposure = sum_l w_l * frac_neighbors_wearing_l.

adoption_rule.source: Model design choice informed by data
adoption_rule.notes: Use logistic: Pr(M_t=1)=sigma(theta0 + gamma*M_{t-1} + beta_info*I_{t-1} + sum_l lambda_l*frac_l + group and risk terms).

group_modifiers.notes: Estimate fixed effects or interactions; apply as additive or multiplicative modifiers.

info_arrival_rate.notes: Use observed time series; optionally allow group-specific rates.

info_network_spread.notes: If evidence that info depends on peers, include neighbor_info_fraction effect; otherwise treat info as exogenous.

noise_variance.notes: Evaluate overdispersion; add idiosyncratic shocks if needed.

preprocessing_steps.step: Clean and type-cast IDs across files
preprocessing_steps.purpose: Ensure agent_id alignment (int vs string) for joins and network construction.
Build family, work_school, community adjacency; deduplicate, remove self-loops, symmetrize.

preprocessing_steps.step: Compute per-layer neighbor signals per agent-day
preprocessing_steps.purpose: For each day, compute frac_neighbors_wearing_t-1 overall and by layer to use as regressors.
Join agent_attributes to panel; standardize or transform risk_perception (e.g., logit) and one-hot encode groups.
Add wearing_mask_t-1 and received_info_t-1 (and optionally t) to model short-term dynamics.

preprocessing_steps.step: Split data into calibration/validation periods and/or agents
preprocessing_steps.purpose: Hold out final days or a subset of agents for out-of-sample validation.

calibration_strategy.calibration_approach: Use a two-stage approach. Stage 1: Estimate behavioral coefficients with a panel logistic regression (or mixed-effects model) for Pr(M_t=1) with predictors M_{t-1}, I_{t-1}, neighbor_mask_fraction_{t-1} (overall and by layer), risk_perception, age_group, occupation, and interactions (e.g., risk x neighbor). Include agent random intercepts or fixed effects to absorb unobserved heterogeneity. Extract coefficients to map into agent rules (baseline propensity, habit, info effect, layer-specific influence). Stage 2: Perform simulated method of moments (SMM) or approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) to fine-tune network layer weights and threshold/susceptibility distributions so simulated trajectories match observed moments: overall prevalence by day, subgroup prevalence (age_group x occupation), transition rates, and spatial/network clustering metrics. Optionally cross-validate layer weights and group modifiers.
calibration_strategy.validation_strategy: Validate on held-out days or agents by comparing: (1) daily prevalence curves (overall and stratified), (2) transition probabilities (on->on, off->on given info/no-info), (3) correlation between predicted and observed adoption at node and subgroup levels, (4) network-local Moran’s I or assortativity of adoption, and (5) calibration residual diagnostics. Conduct sensitivity analyses on layer weights and homophily. Use rolling-origin time splits to assess temporal generalization.
key_variables_to_calibrate: network_influence_strength (lambda overall and lambda_l per layer)

Semantic metadata summary for agent_attributes.csv

- Overall data structure and type
  - CSV, flat tabular file; one row per agent.
  - Primary key: agent_id (unique integer). No nested structures.

- Meaning of keys/columns
  - agent_id: Unique identifier for an individual agent; use to link with network edges/contacts in other files.
  - age_group: Categorical demographic segment (e.g., Youth, Young Adult, Middle Age); can proxy different mixing patterns and responsiveness to norms/policies.
  - occupation: Categorical role (e.g., Student, Blue Collar, White Collar); indicates primary social context (school, workplace) and contact layer.
  - risk_perception: Float in [0,1]; baseline perceived health risk. Higher values imply greater intrinsic propensity to wear masks absent social influence.

- Relationships or nested elements
  - No nested elements within the file.
  - Intended relational joins via agent_id to:
    - Network topology (who interacts with whom).
    - Context layers (e.g., school/workplace/community) inferred from occupation and possibly age_group.
  - age_group and occupation support homophily and layer-specific contact rates; they can condition influence strength and exposure frequency.

- How this data should inform simulation entities or interactions
  - Agent initialization: For each row, create an agent with attributes {age_group, occupation, risk_perception} and a mask_wearing state variable.
  - Network construction: Use occupation and age_group to assign agents to layers (school, workplace, community) and to tune homophily when generating edges.
  - Behavioral dynamics:
    - Set initial mask-wearing probability or threshold as a function of risk_perception.
    - Modulate susceptibility to social influence and compliance costs by age_group/occupation.
    - Allow risk_perception to interact with peer behavior and external signals to update mask_wearing over time.
  - Reporting/stratification: Track adoption rates and dynamics by age_group and occupation for outcome analysis.

Semantic metadata summary for social_network.json (for mask-wearing diffusion simulation)

- Data structure and type
  - JSON object (dictionary) where each top-level key is an agent/node ID (as a string).
  - Each value is an object with three arrays: family, work_school, community.
  - Arrays contain integers representing IDs of other agents.

- Meaning of keys/columns
  - Top-level keys: unique agent identifiers.
  - Nested keys:
    - family: household/kinship ties.
    - work_school: workplace or school ties.
    - community: broader community/social ties (neighbors, friends, public contacts).
  - Array values: adjacency lists of neighbors on that specific layer; unweighted, no timestamps.

- Relationships and nesting
  - Multiplex (multi-layer) social network: same set of agents connected via three distinct tie types.
  - Edges are given as adjacency lists; directionality is not guaranteed (links may need symmetrization).
  - Overlap across layers is possible (the same neighbor can appear in multiple layers).
  - No edge attributes (e.g., strength, frequency) or node attributes included.

- Implications for simulation entities/interactions
  - Agents: instantiate one agent per top-level key; store agent state (e.g., mask_wearing, susceptibility, conformity) separately.
  - Network layers: build three graphs from the adjacency lists (family, work_school, community). Consider casting node IDs to int to match neighbor lists.
  - Interaction modeling:
    - Sample contacts per timestep within each layer; optionally assign layer weights/frequencies (e.g., family > work_school > community) to reflect stronger influence/probability of interaction at home.
    - Influence/diffusion rules (e.g., threshold, contagion, or Bayesian updating) should aggregate neighbor signals per layer with layer-specific weights.
  - Preprocessing recommendations:
    - Validate that all neighbor IDs exist as nodes; deduplicate lists; remove self-loops.
    - Decide on directed vs. undirected model; if undirected is desired, symmetrize adjacency.
    - Optionally compute per-layer degrees/centrality for seeding strategies and analysis.
  - Limitations to address with assumptions/config:
    - No temporal dynamics or contact frequencies provided; must be specified in simulation parameters.
    - No demographic or attribute data; if needed, synthesize or import from another source.

Semantic metadata summary for train_data.csv

- Overall structure and type
  - CSV (tabular, tidy/panel format).
  - Each row is an agent–day observation (long format time series).
  - Composite primary key: (day, agent_id).

- Column meanings
  - day: Integer timestep (discrete daily schedule).
  - agent_id: Unique identifier for an agent (stable across days).
  - wearing_mask: Boolean state of the agent on that day (behavior/adoption).
  - received_info: Boolean state indicating whether the agent received pro-mask information/exposure on that day.

- Relationships and nesting
  - No nested structures; repeated rows per agent across days.
  - Temporal dependency within agent trajectories (state transitions from day t to t+1).
  - Potential relational join point to an external social network (e.g., adjacency list/matrix) via agent_id; network topology is not included here.

- Implications for the simulation
  - Defines the agent set (unique agent_id values) and the discrete-time update cadence (daily).
  - Provides observable state variables to initialize day 0 and to calibrate/validate transition dynamics:
    - Adoption dynamics: P(wearing_mask_t+1 | wearing_mask_t, received_info_t, possibly neighbors’ states).
    - Information diffusion: P(received_info_t+1 | prior info state, network exposure, external seeding).
  - Guides scheduling: synchronous daily updates of agent states.
  - Requires an external or synthetic social network to model peer influence; not present in the file.
  - Can be used to estimate parameters (e.g., influence of information on adoption, persistence/decay of wearing, baseline adoption without info) and to compare simulated trajectories to observed panel data.
